passage: In the college library's discussion room, Uma had the project tracker open on her laptop. Four names, twelve tasks. "Ritvik gets nothing this time," she said. Jaya looked up. "Nothing? He's in the group." "He sent the literature review a day late in week two. I had to stay up formatting everything. I'm not risking the final report on him." "He had fever that week, remember?" "Still." Uma left his row empty and split his tasks between herself and Jaya. When Ritvik messaged offering to do the survey charts, she replied, "Covered, thanks." Later, alone in the room, she noticed that the charts he'd made for the midterm were the neatest in the whole file. She scrolled past them quickly.

qa.q: Why does Uma say Ritvik gets nothing this time?
qa.a: He sent the literature review a day late in week two, and she had to stay up formatting everything.

qa.q: Why does leaving Ritvik's row empty feel sensible to Uma?
qa.a: After losing sleep over his late part, Uma wants to protect the final report, so cutting him out feels like being careful rather than unfair.

qa.q: What could Uma do instead of scrolling past his charts?
qa.a: She could weigh his whole record, including the neat midterm charts and his fever, and give him the survey charts with a clear deadline.

qa.q: How might Jaya feel about suddenly carrying Ritvik's share?
qa.a: Jaya may feel uneasy, since she remembers he was ill and now has extra work because of a judgement she questioned.

grounding: A student lets one late submission define a groupmate and stops giving him work despite his neat charts.

passage:
Hi Minakshi,
Quick update from the hostel. Remember Aniket from my design project group? I've basically taken him off everything. He missed the first mock-up deadline by a whole day, and after that I just can't trust him. I've given his wireframes to Kavin and I'm doing the presentation slides myself.
Today he asked in the group chat if he could handle the user interviews. I said we'd already sorted it. Honestly it's easier this way. Although... Kavin told me Aniket's interview notes last semester were the best in the class, and that he'd been travelling home for a wedding that week. I don't know. I'm tired, and it's simpler not to depend on him.
Write soon,
Sharmila

qa.q: Who got Aniket's wireframes?
qa.a: Sharmila gave his wireframes to Kavin.

qa.q: What is Sharmila feeling when writing 'it's easier this way'?
qa.a: Sharmila sounds tired and wants to avoid another let-down, so leaning on nobody feels safer than giving Aniket a second chance.

qa.q: What would you advise Sharmila about the user interviews?
qa.a: Since Aniket's interview notes were the best in the class, Sharmila could give him that task with a check-in date instead of judging him by one late mock-up.

qa.q: How might Aniket experience being told everything is already sorted?
qa.a: Aniket may feel pushed out of his own project without knowing why, especially if he thinks the wedding trip explained the delay.

grounding: In an email, a student admits to writing off a groupmate after one late deadline and no longer giving him tasks.

passage: Okay, Sangeeta, you asked why Deven isn't doing anything in our marketing project. Honestly? Second week, he submitted the survey summary late. One day late. The professor marked the whole group down by two points. From that moment I decided he's just not dependable. I stopped assigning him anything and did his part myself. Now it's week nine, I'm exhausted, and he keeps saying, "Give me something, anything." My mother always says, "Lakshmi, you hold grudges like a bank holds gold." Maybe. But what if he's late again? I did check: he's been on time for every other assignment this term. It's just that one day keeps replaying in my head, louder than everything else.

qa.q: How many points did the professor take off for the late summary?
qa.a: The professor marked the whole group down by two points.

qa.q: What worry keeps Lakshmi from giving Deven any work?
qa.a: Lakshmi keeps thinking 'what if he's late again?', so that one day feels louder than all his on-time work. 😰

qa.q: What could Lakshmi try now, in week nine?
qa.a: Lakshmi could hand Deven one clear task with an early deadline and judge him on his whole term's record, not just week two.

qa.q: What is it like for Deven to keep asking for work?
qa.a: Deven is probably frustrated and embarrassed, shut out of his own project for one late day while he pleads, 'Give me something, anything.'

grounding: A student explains how one late submission made the speaker write off a groupmate and do all his work.

passage:
I'm Ishita, and I shared a project group with Aditi and two others this semester. In week two, Karthik submitted his part of the market survey a day late. He said sorry in the group chat. Aditi didn't reply.
At the next meeting she divided the tasks on the whiteboard. Karthik's name had nothing beside it. "It's fine, I'll do the analysis myself," she said. "We can't risk another delay." When Karthik offered to draft the slides, she said she'd already started them.
By week six he'd stopped offering. At the final review, the professor asked him a question about the survey and he answered it better than any of us. Aditi looked surprised.
I don't know what was going on in her mind. From where I sat, it looked like that one late day had become the whole story of Karthik for her.

qa.q: What did Karthik submit a day late in week two?
qa.a: He submitted his part of the market survey a day late.

qa.q: Why might giving Karthik nothing have felt sensible to Aditi?
qa.a: She was worried about another delay hurting the project, so after one late submission it felt safer to take his work herself than to trust him again.

qa.q: What went wrong in the group, and what could have fixed it?
qa.a: One late day made Aditi stop giving Karthik any tasks, and he stopped offering; giving him a small task with a clear deadline would have let the group see what he could actually do.

qa.q: How might Karthik have experienced weeks two to six?
qa.a: Karthik probably felt pushed out after apologising, which may explain why he stopped offering, even though he understood the survey better than anyone.

grounding: Told by a groupmate, it shows a student writing off a group member after one late submission and taking all tasks from him.

passage:
Monday. The design brief was due at noon, and Jomon's part came in at 4 p.m. Avni read it on the hostel stairs and texted the group: "Great. Now we look careless." Jomon's reply, "sorry, bus broke down," she left unread.
Thursday. At the planning meeting in the library, Avni wrote out the next tasks. Research: Avni. Sketches: Avni and Bina. Presentation: Bina. Jomon, sitting at the end of the table, asked, "What should I take?" Avni said, "Just review it when it's done." He closed his laptop.
Two weeks later. The group presented to their tutor. Avni had slept four hours. Jomon sat in the back row of the studio with nothing on the slides carrying his name. When the tutor asked who had done the costing, nobody had, and Avni realised it had once been on Jomon's list.

qa.q: At what time did Jomon's part come in on Monday?
qa.a: Jomon's part came in at 4 p.m.

qa.q: What was Avni worried about when she saw the late submission?
qa.a: She worried the group would now look careless, and she felt that one late part meant Jomon could not be trusted with anything important.

qa.q: What could Avni have done at the Thursday meeting instead?
qa.a: She could have heard his reason and given Jomon a clear task with an early check-in, instead of letting one late part decide that he got no work at all.

qa.q: How does the situation look from Jomon's side by the presentation?
qa.a: For Jomon it seems he was shut out after one late day, sitting in the back with nothing carrying his name, and the costing that had been his task never got done.

grounding: Across three beats it shows a student writing off a group member after one late submission, so the single flaw becomes his whole story.
